AMEND AND RECOMMIT TO VETERANS, HOMELAND SECURITY AND MILITARY AFFAIRS
COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES

items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the penal law and the executive law, in relation to acts of
terrorism and the New York state intelligence center
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S7813

SPONSOR: MURPHY
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the penal law and the executive law,
in relation to acts of terrorism and the New York state intelligence
center

 
PURPOSE:

Includes mass shootings with the definition of an act of terrorism

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one of the bill contains legislative findings which include the
mass shootings in San Bernadino, California and Charleston, South Caro-
lina in 2015, the Orlando nightclub in 2016, the Las Vegas strip in
2017, and at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida
in 2018, among others within state terrorism statute, because those
shootings are different than the instances of terrorism presently
described in that section. The courts will then judge future applica-
tions of any new statute with that in mind.

Section two of the bill amends subdivision 1 of Section 490.05 of Title
Y-1 of Part 4 of the penal law to include individuals who knowingly,
within a distance of 1,000 feet from the grounds of a public, parochial
or private school, within a distance of 1,000 feet from the place of a
grounds of worship, or in a place of business with one or more employ-
ees, discharge or attempt to discharge a firearm.

Section three of the bill amends subdivision 1 of Section 490.25 of
Title Y-1 of Part 4 of the penal law to clarify a "school, house of
warship or business" as areas protected when the defendant intends to
"affect the conduct" of those areas in the context of terrorism cases.

Section four of the bill adds a new article 26-a to the executive law to
govern the New York State Intelligence Center. The bill establishes the
intelligence center within the Division of Homeland Security to collect,
integrate, evaluate, analyze, disseminate and maintain criminal intelli-
gence information to aid in detecting, preventing, investigating and
responding to terrorism. The center shall cooperate with the division of
state police, local state and federal government agencies, subject to
applicable state and federal laws and regulations, in the collection of
criminal intelligence information, only if reasonable suspicion exists
that the subject of the information or is involved with or has knowledge
of criminal or terrorist activity. Papers, records, documents, reports,
materials, databases, or other evidence or information relative to crim-
inal intelligence or any terrorism investigation in the possession of
the New York State Intelligence Center shall be confidential and shall
not be subject to the Freedom of Information Law. Any person who know-
ingly disseminates information maintained by the Center without prior
authorization shall be guilty of a Class A misdemeanor. If such unau-
thorized dissemination results in death or serious bodily injury to
another person, such person is guilty of a Class D felony. No cause of
action for defamation, invasion of privacy, or negligence shall arise
against any person for reason of that person's furnishing of information
concerning any suspected, anticipated, or completed criminal violation
when the information is provided to or received from the Division or any
federal or state governmental entity established for the purposes of
detecting and preventing acts of terrorism. The division shall not
collect, maintain or share with any other law enforcement agency, infor-
mation about the political, religious or social associations, views or
activities of a person unless the information directly relates to an
investigation of criminal conduct and there are reasonable grounds to
believe that the subject of the information is involved in the criminal
conduct.  Information about a person's political, religious or social
associations, views or activities that is collected or maintained by the
division shall be destroyed if a criminal charge, to which the informa-
tion is material or directly related, is not brought against the person
within a reasonable period of time. The division shall provide an annual
report to the attorney general describing all information collected,
maintained or shared by the agency on the political, religious or social
associations, views or activities of a person. The attorney general
shall have access to the files and records of a law enforcement agency
to oversee and monitor compliance.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

All perceived violence that threaten the lives of others, whether at a
concert, place of worship or school, are terroristic threats, and must
be handled in the same manner. Mass shooting should be prioritized in
the same manner as other acts of terror. This means enacting stiffer
penalties, establishing a framework for intelligence collection and
sharing between federal, state and local partners, and encompassing the
prevention of mass shootings within New York State's counterterrorism
efforts. Such measures are not about going after gun rights. Rather they
are designed to ensure that just as our counterterrorism efforts are
focused ensuring that another 9/11 can never be allowed to happen again,
there should be commensurate measures in place to ensure other kinds of
mass casualty events, geared at intimidating and terrorizing the civil-
ian populace receive the same attention.  As Uri Friedman of The Atlan-
tic recently observed in 'The U.S. Fights Terrorism-But Not School
Shooting' the U.S. government has made a serious response to terrorism
in the wake of 9/11. Friedman noted that "Terrorist attacks and mass
shootings are distinct phenomena-though, as in the 2016 Orlando night-
club shooting, they occasionally overlap. (One in five terrorist attacks
in the United States between 2002 and 2016 involved firearms.) Terrorism
is typically directed or inspired by specific organizations that serial-
ly practice violence for political ends and that attack not just indi-
viduals but society. It's therefore challenging to compare with mass
shootings, whose damage is usually measured in casualty counts and which
can have a range of motivations. But both are rare yet recurring, terri-
fying, and to a considerable extent preventable acts of mass
destruction. And even if you add all the caveats you want to the statis-
tics showing that the number of Americans killed by terrorism in the
post-9/11 period is a fraction of the number of Americans killed by mass
shootings, it's hard to avoid one conclusion: In terms of action and
investment, there is a colossal gap in how the U.S. federal government
has prioritized stopping one form of aberrant violence versus the
other."

This legislation classifies mass shootings as acts of terror to better
safeguard society against future threats.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

AN ACT to amend the penal law and the executive law, in relation to acts of
terrorism and the New York state intelligence center
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S7813A

SPONSOR: MURPHY
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the penal law and the executive law,
in relation to acts of terrorism and the New York state intelligence
center

 
PURPOSE:

This bill would include intentionally discharging a firearm within 1000
feet of a school, a place of worship, or a mass gathering of 25 or more
people, an act of terrorism under the penal law, and would codify the
operations of the New York State Intelligence Center under the direction
and purview of the state police.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one of the bill adds the mass shootings in San Bernadino, Cali-
fornia and Charleston, South Carolina in 2015, the Orlando nightclub in
2016, the Las Vegas strip in 2017, and at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High
School in Parkland, Florida in 2018, to the legislative findings, as
examples included within the state terrorism statute.

Section two of the bill amends Section 490.05 of the penal law to
include individuals who knowingly, unlawfully, discharge a firearm with-
in 1000 feet of a school, a place of worship, or a mass gathering of 25
or more people, or in a business of one or more employees, with the
definition of committing an act of terrorism.

Section three of the bill amends Section 490.25 of the penal law to
clarify a "school, house of worship, business or mass gathering" as
areas protected when the defendant intends to "affect the conduct" of
those areas in the context of terrorism cases.

Section four of the bill adds a new Article 26-A to the executive law,
to codify the operations of the New York State Intelligence Center.  The
new Article establishes the intelligence center within the Division of
State Police. Pursuant to its provisions, the New York State Intelli-
gence Center would be responsible for the collection, integration,
receipt, processing, evaluation, analysis, fusing, dissemination, shar-
ing, and maintenance of intelligence information to aid in detecting,
preventing, investigating and responding to acts of terrorism.

This new Article would further provide that the center would cooperate
with the state division of homeland security and emergency services, and
other state, local, and federal government agencies, subject to applica-
ble state and federal laws, rules and regulations.

This new Article would also, for the first time, provide that schools
and the state department of education would be participating parties at
the intelligence center, and would further add a new Buffalo office to
the current fusion centers in Albany and New York City.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

All perceived violence that threaten the lives of others, whether at a
concert, place of worship or school, are terroristic threats, and must
be viewed, under law, in the same manner. Mass shootings should be
prioritized in the same way as other acts of terror. This means enacting
stiffer penalties, establishing a framework for intelligence collection,
analysis and information sharing between federal, state and local part-
ners, and encompassing the prevention of mass shootings within New York
State's counterterrorism efforts.

Such measures are not about going after gun rights. Rather they are
designed to ensure that just as our counterterrorism efforts are focused
on ensuring that another 9/11 can never be allowed to happen again, that
there should be and equal and commensurate effort in place to ensure
that other kinds of mass casualty events, such as a horrific school
shooting, receive the same attention and law enforcement mobilization
and priorities.

This bill seeks to close the gap between how the government addresses
mass shoot events and terrorist attacks. The two are integrally inter-
related, and our level of concern to protect our children in their
school environment, needs to be elevated to the same degree as we have
improved public protection at airports. We need to focus our intelli-
gence and law enforcement resources in both arenas, so as to improve the
safeguards for all the public at all venues. Danger and threats have
many facets, and by improving terrorism prevention, response and recov-
ery to also explicitly include mass shootings, this bill will go a long
way to improving public protection for all the citizens of the state of
New York.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New Bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediately.
